background.definition: RAS is the narrowing of the renal artery caused by atherosclerosis or fibromuscular hyperplasia.

list.listitem: Among asymptomatic community dwelling persons over 65 years of age with normal renal arteries at baseline, only 4% develop significant RAS 8 years later (0.5% per year).
Using a population-based registry of patients with end stage renal disease (ESRD), the incidence of ESRD attributed to RAS is about 6 per 100,000 per year.
Among asymptomatic community dwelling persons over 65 years of age, about 7% have significant RAS (88% unilateral) on duplex ultrasonography.
Among patients with hypertension, about 1% have RAS.
Up to 60% of patients with peripheral artery disease have significant RAS.
In patients undergoing cardiac catheterization, significant RAS is present in 10%-15% of patients with coronary artery stenosis.
Atherosclerosis causes the majority of stenotic renal arteries.
Fibromuscular dysplasia is the second most common cause of RAS.
Rarely, direct injury from trauma, compression, or radiation injury; autoimmune disorders like Takayasu's arteritis; retroperitoneal fibrosis; neurofibromatosis.
RAS increases plasma renin activity which increases blood pressure.

Since renal blood flow and glomerular filtration are partially maintained by angiotensin II vasoconstriction of the renal arterioles, the administration of angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors and angiotensin receptor blockers can cause acute renal failure by decreasing the glomerular perfusion pressure which reduces filtration.
Suspect RAS in patients with hypertension if it is: diagnosed before age 30; uncontrolled on 3 or more medications in those over 55. C
Additionally, suspect RAS in patients with accelerated or malignant hypertension. C

Patients with suspected RAS should undergo non-invasive imaging: duplex ultrasound, computed tomographic angiography (CTA) in individuals with normal renal function, or magnetic resonance angiography (MRA). C
RAS is largely an asymptomatic condition.
About 1/3 of patients with renovascular hypertension have abdominal bruits.
A systolic/diastolic bruit is highly specific but relatively insensitive for detecting renovascular hypertension.
RAS is often an incidental finding in patients undergoing angiography for other conditions.

Patients with suspected RAS should undergo non-invasive imaging: duplex ultrasound, CTA in individuals with normal renal function, MRA. These tests have largely replaced plasma renin assays.
Renal duplex ultrasound: In a systematic review of 88 studies that evaluated nearly 10,000 arteries in over 8,000 patients, compared with findings on angiography, renal duplex ultrasound was 85% sensitive and 92% specific. MRA: In a systematic review of 25 studies that evaluated nearly 1000 patients with MRA and angiography, non-enhanced MRA was 94% sensitive (95% CI, 90%-97%) and 85% specific (95% CI, 82%-87%). Gadolinium enhanced MRA was 97% sensitive (95% CI, 93%-98%) and its specificity was 93% (95% CI, 91%-95%). CT angiography: In a systematic review of 22 studies, the sensitivity of CTA was between 94% and 100% and its specificity between 65% and 99%.
When non-invasive tests are inconclusive in a patient with a high clinical index of suspicion, catheter angiography may be used as a diagnostic test.

Captopril renal scintigraphy, selective renal vein renin measurements, plasma renin activity, and captopril test measure of plasma renin are not recommended as a screening tests to establish the diagnosis of RAS.

A clinical rule has been developed to predict the likelihood of RAS among patients with difficult to control hypertension. Key predictors include smoking, recent onset hypertension, hyperlipidemia, bruit, comorbid cardiovascular disease, and gender.
Suspect RAS in patients with hypertension if it is: diagnosed before age 30; uncontrolled on 3 or more medications in those over 55; accelerated or malignant hypertension.

Additional situations in which RAS should be suspected: patients with significant atherosclerosis; onset of new or worsening azotemia after using an ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker; unexplained pulmonary edema or congestive heart failure unexplained renal impairment; atrophic kidney or more than 1.5 cm difference in size.
See for a suggested approach to managing the patient with RAS.
Patients with hypertension associated with RAS can be treated with the same medications used to treat essential hypertension. B
The results of several small RCTs are inconclusive regarding balloon angioplasty in patients whose blood pressure can be controlled with medication. A
In patients with bilateral RAS, those treated with balloon angioplasty had greater improvements in creatinine clearance and blood pressure control than those treated medically. B

Consider referral for angioplasty in patients with hemodynamically significant RAS associated with uncontrolled or accelerated hypertension, hypertension associated with a small kidney, renal dysfunction, recurrent unexplained pulmonary edema or congestive heart failure. B
No medications directly treat RAS.

Patients with hypertension associated with RAS can be treated with the same medications used to treat essential hypertension. Recent recommendations for medical therapy are found in the Joint National Committee (JNC)-8 report.

Few randomized trials have compared medical therapy with angioplasty using stents. One study (using concealed allocation) randomized patients with RAS to percutaneous revascularization versus medical therapy. Revascularization was not superior to medical therapy with regard to renal function, blood pressure control or other major clinical outcomes.

Only a few small randomized trials have compared balloon angioplasty (without stenting) with medical therapy for hypertension in patients with RAS. The results are inconclusive in patients whose blood pressure can be controlled with medication.

Some experts recommend percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stenting over angioplasty without stents in patients with RAS. In a randomized trial, 85 patients with RAS were randomized to angioplasty or angioplasty with stent. Restenosis at 6 months occurred in 48% of patients with angioplasty and 14% of those with stents (NNT = 4) while the rate of complications was about the same. Twelve patients treated without stents had to have a repeat intervention within 6 months. A randomized trial of 140 patients with RAS found that stent placement had no clear benefit vs medical treatment for slowing progression of renal insufficiency and led to an increase in complications including death. Most recently a clinical trial compared stenting versus medical therapy for RAS, finding no added benefit in the stenting group in outcomes.Data from the largest clinical trial showed no significant impact of renal artery stenting on blood pressure or renal artery hemodynamics.

A systematic review of randomized trials comparing percutaneous transluminal angioplasty with stent placement found a low quality of evidence, and no clear benefit compared with medical therapy in terms of kidney function, mortality, cardiovascular events, or need for renal replacement therapy.
Open revascularization, largely replaced by percutaneous procedures even in patients with fibromuscular dysplasia, should be reserved for patients who fail angioplasty.

Evidence is lacking to support the notion that revascularizing patients with renal artery stenosis reduces the risk of recurrent cardiac events including heart failure or non-fatal myocardial infarction.
The rate of progression in RAS depends on the baseline level of severity. About 30% of patients with mild stenosis develop significant stenosis after 1 year. B
Angioplasty improves glomerular filtration in patients with renal dysfunction. B
The average life expectancy of patients with RAS who develop end-stage renal disease is less than 3 years. B

In a cohort of 76 patients (mean age 67) evaluated with duplex ultrasound serially for 3 years, only 8% of those with normal renal arteries at baseline progressed to significant stenosis (more than 60% occlusion) after 3 years.
Among patients with mild stenosis (less than 60%) at baseline, 30% will develop significant stenosis after 1 year, 44% after 2 years, and 48% after 3 years.
Among patients with significant stenosis (greater than 60%) at baseline, 4% will totally occlude after 1 and 2 years, and 7% after 3 years.
After 2 years of follow-up, about 3% of patients with unilateral RAS, 18% of patients with bilateral RAS, and almost 60% of patients with RAS in a solitary kidney will require dialysis.
The average life expectancy of patients with RAS who develop end-stage renal disease is less than 3 years.

In a retrospective study of 144 patients with RAS and accelerating hypertension, 12 months after undergoing angioplasty, those with accelerating hypertension reduced the number of medications from 3 to 2.5.
In the same study, angioplasty improved glomerular filtration in patients with renal dysfunction. In spite of this, those patients with baseline creatinine over 3.4 mg/dL had lower survival rates.

cell.label: Suspicion of renal artery stenosis: Perform duplex ultrasound, MR angiogram, or CT angiogram (if patient has normal kidney function).
Options: (1) treat medically and monitor, or (2) refer for angioplasty if there is a single ipsilateral viable kidney, bilateral stenosis, or unilateral stenosis and chronic renal insufficiency.
Options: (1) treat medically and monitor, or (2) refer for arteriogram if index of suspicion is high.

footnotes.footnote: *Symptomatic denotes any of the following: uncontrolled, accelerated or malignant hypertension; hypertension with unilateral small kidney; recurrent unexplained congestive heart failure or sudden unexplained pulmonary edema; chronic renal insufficiency with unilateral stenosis to a solitary functioning kidney; chronic renal insufficiency with bilateral stenosis; or unstable angina.
